title: Coding Workflow Example & Question
author: zatsnotmyname
selftext:
I mainly use Claude Code.  I use a mix of an old Mini-PC and a Strix Halo 128gb PC as my AI workers and coordinaters.  Not really using the Strix for actual inference yet, but have Halogen set up, and have used it a bunch for regression & perf testing.

Since game design is so interactive, and I am innovating in my games, rather than just cloning or doing generic things, I find I am going back and forth a bunch with a single or maybe two sessions on my projects, which is pretty slow and I rarely get the AIs working for hours except for long regression sessions.

I get jealous when I read about web developers being able to have the agents coordinating and doing all these tasks autonomously, and I was wondering how I could get some of that for my uses.

So, last night I decided to rename my main Claude Code game session 'Game Worker' and made a separate one called 'Game Producer'.  I then talk only  to the Producer.  I can chat with her back and forth and talk priorities and tradeoffs, and then she instructs the Worker on how to prioritize, etc.  Seems to work better.

Once I got this working on Game 1, I have asked Game2 Producer to talk to Game 1 Producer to get her workflow, which involves an inbox folder that contains the task info and priorities.

Right now I have 3 Producers coordinating access to my Google TV so they can use it to test out the game performance on it.

Would love to hear : 

* How I'm an idiot and should be using XYZ Claude feature or skill instead
* How you are managing projects
* How you are managing multiple projects
* How you are having your projects learn from each other and improve workflow over time

comments.author: 2ko2ko2
comments.body: Personally, I prefer the slower method of talking back and forth with claude as it implements my decisions (like you were doing before) instead of relying on an AI to make those decisions. Mostly cause I want to understand what code it is implementing (If I don't understand what it does I can just ask claude to explain it to me). I have on multiple occasions been able to bring up questions or areas of the design it may have not fully understood (due to my own lack of explanation earlier on) that has lead to revisions in the code claude ended up implementing that more aligned with my vision. Also, I see myself as a designer not a producer. I want to be making all of these micro-decisions that shape the overall design rather than giving the AI a vague idea of what I want and trusting that it both understands what I want completely (unlikely, there are always small details you'll either forget to bring up or that you don't even think of in the moment) and knows how to implement what I want. I'm not saying it's impossible for the more agentic approach to work (where you have agents talking to each other to make decisions on your behalf), but from everything I've seen on this sub and the claudegamedev sub, it tends to lead to more generic designs overall.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
I do something close to your Producer/Worker split, just inside one session. The main session is the one I talk to: it plans, decides what to build and checks the results. The actual coding goes out to cheaper sub-agents with one complete brief each, and small chores like commits go to the smallest model.

Two things made it work. The brief has to carry everything up front (the task, why, what not to touch, how it will be checked), because topping it up with follow-up messages went worse every time. And the main session checks the work itself, by running the tests or looking at the page, never just taking the worker's "done" for it.

For multiple projects, each one has a single handoff file at the root that gets rewritten at every stopping point, so any session in any project can pick up cold.
